articles_used.summary_raw: The meeting comes with challenges as there are things Xi does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
articles_used.full_text:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summit
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fourth year, to be on the agenda.
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fourth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives
The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.
Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.
Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.
The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.
The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race.  The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.
Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.
Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.
China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025
This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.
Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.
Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.
But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.
Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.
There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.
Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.
The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.
So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.
For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.
But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.
A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy
He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.
A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.
Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.
At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

Aufgrund eines neuen ukrainischen Angriffs ist der Zugverkehr über die Krim-Brücke nach Angaben der russischen Besatzungsbehörden "vorerst" eingestellt worden. "Der entstandene Schaden wird derzeit ermittelt", teilte der von Moskau eingesetzte Verwaltungschef, Sergej Aksjonow, bei Telegram mit. Alle zuständigen Stellen seien im Einsatz, eine Schadensbegutachtung sei "im Gange".
Es ist der dritte Angriff in dieser Woche auf die Brücke, die das russische Festland mit der 2014 von Moskau annektierten ukrainischen Halbinsel Krim verbindet. Fortunes are madeby entrepreneurs and investors when revolutionary technologies enable waves of innovative, investable companies. Think of the railroad, the Bessemer process, electric power, the internal combustion engine, or the microprocessor—each of which, like a stray spark in a fireworks factory, set off decades of follow-on innovations, permeated every part of society, and catapulted a new set of inventors and investors into power, influence, and wealth.
Yet some technological innovations, though societally transformative, generate little in the way of new wealth; instead, they reinforce the status quo. Fifteen years before the microprocessor, another revolutionary idea, shipping containerization, arrived at a less propitious time, when technological advancement was a Red Queen’s race, and inventors and investors were left no better off for non-stop running.
Anyone who invests in thenewnew thing must answer two questions: First, how much value will this innovation create? And second, who will capture it? Information and communication technology (ICT) was a revolution whose value was captured by startups and led to thousands of newly rich founders, employees, and investors. In contrast, shipping containerization was a revolution whose value was spread so thin that in the end, it made only a single founder temporarily rich and only a single investor a little bit richer.
Is generative AI more like the former or the latter? Will it be the basis of many future industrial fortunes, or a net loser for the investment community as a whole, with a few zero-sum winners here and there?
There are ways to make money investing in the fruits of AI, but they will depend on assuming the latter—that it is once again a less propitious time for inventors and investors, that AI model builders and application companies will eventually compete each other into an oligopoly, and that the gains from AI will accrue not to its builders but to customers. A lot of the money pouring into AI is therefore being invested in the wrong places, and aside from a couple of lucky early investors, those who make money will be the ones with the foresight to get out early.
The microprocessor was revolutionary, but the people who invented it at Intel in 1971 did not see it that way—they just wanted to avoid designing desktop calculator chipsets from scratch every time. But outsiders realized they could use the microprocessor to build their own personal computers, and enthusiasts did. Thousands of tinkerers found configurations and uses that Intel never dreamed of. This distributed and permissionless invention kicked off a “great surge of development,” as the economist Carlota Perez calls it, triggered by technology but driven by economic and societal forces.[1]
There was no real demand for personal computers in the early 1970s; they were expensive toys. But the experimenters laid the technical groundwork and built a community. Then, around 1975, a step-change in the cost of microprocessors made the personal computer market viable. The Intel 8080 had an initial list price of $360 ($2,300 in today’s dollars). MITS could barely turn a profit on its Altair at a bulk price of $75 each ($490 today). But when MOS Technologies started selling its 6502 for $25 ($150 today), Steve Wozniak could afford to build a prototype Apple. The 6502 and the similarly priced Zilog Z80 forced Intel’s prices down. The nascent PC community started spawning entrepreneurs and a score of companies appeared, each with a slightly different product.
You couldn’t have known in the mid-1970s that the PC (and PC-like products, such as ATMs, POS terminals, smartphones, etc.) would revolutionize everything. While Steve Jobs was telling investors that every household would someday have a personal computer (a wild underestimate, as it turned out), others questioned the need for personal computers at all. As late as 1979, Apple’s ads didn’t tell you what a personal computer could do—itaskedwhat you did with it.[2]The established computer manufacturers (IBM, HP, DEC) had no interest in a product their customers weren’t asking for. Nobody “needed” a computer, and so PCs weren’t bought—they were sold. Flashy startups like Apple and Sinclair used hype to get noticed, while companies with footholds in consumer electronics like Atari, Commodore, and Tandy/RadioShack used strong retail connections to put their PCs in front of potential customers.
The market grew slowly at first, accelerating only as experiments led to practical applications like the spreadsheet, introduced in 1979. As use grew, observation of use caused a reduction in uncertainty, leading to more adoption in a self-reinforcing cycle. This kind of gathering momentum takes time in every technological wave: It took almost 30 years for electricity to reach half of American households, for example, and it took about the same amount of time for personal computers.[3]When a technological revolution changes everything, it takes a huge amount of innovation, investment, storytelling, time, and plain old work. It also sucks up all the money and talent available. Like Kuhn’s paradigms in science, any technology not part of the wave’s techno-economic paradigm will seem like a sideshow.[4]
Source:[3]
The nascent growth of PCs attracted investors—venture capitalists—who started making risky bets on new companies. This development incentivized more inventors, entrepreneurs, and researchers, which in turn drew in more speculative capital.
Companies like IBM, the computing behemoth before the PC, saw poor relative performance. They didn’t believe the PC could survive long enough to become capable in their market and didn’t care about new, small markets that wanted a cheaper solution.
Retroactively, we give the PC pioneers the powers of prophets rather than visionaries. But at the time, nobody outside of a small group of early adopters paid any attention. Establishment media likeThe New York Timesdidn’t take the PC seriously until after IBM’s was introduced in August 1981. In the entire year of 1976, when Apple Computer was founded, theNYTmentioned PCs only four times.[5]Apparently, only the crazy ones, the misfits, the rebels, and the troublemakers were paying attention.
Source:[5]
It’s the element of surprise that should strike us most forcefully when we compare the early days of the computer revolution to today. No one took note of personal computers in the 1970s. In 2025, AI is all we seem to talk about.
Big companies hate surprises.That’s why uncertainty makes a perfect moat for startups. Apple would never have survived IBM entering the market in 1979, and only lived to compete another day after raising $100 million in its 1980 IPO. It was the only remaining competitor after the IBM-induced winnowing.[6]
Source:[6]
As the tech took hold and started to show promise, innovations in software, memory, and peripherals like floppy disk drives and modems joined it. They reinforced one another, with each advance putting pressure on the technologies adjacent to it. When any part of the system held back the other parts, investors rushed to fund that sector. As increases in PC memory allowed more complicated software, for example, there became a need for more external storage, which caused VC Dave Marquardt to invest in disk drive manufacturer Seagate in 1980. Seagate gave Marquardt a 40x return when it went public in 1981. Other investors noticed, and some $270 million was plowed into the industry in the following three years.[7]
Money also poured into the underlying infrastructure—fiber optic networks, chip making, etc.—so that capacity was never a bottleneck. Companies which used the new technological system to outperform incumbents began to take market share, and even staid competitors realized they needed to adopt the new thing or die. The hype became a froth which became an investment bubble: the dot-com frenzy of the late 1990s. The ICT wave was therefore similar to previous ones—like the investment mania of the 1830s and the Roaring ‘20s, which followed the infrastructure buildout of canals and railways, respectively—in which the human response to each stage predictably generated the next.
When the dot-com bubble popped, society found it disapproved of the excesses in the sector and governments found they had the popular support to reassert authority over the tech companies and their investors. This put a brake on the madness. Instead of the reckless innovation of the bubble, companies started to expand into proven markets, and financiers moved from speculating to investing. Entrepreneurs began to focus on finding applications rather than on innovating the underlying technologies. Technological improvements continued, but change became more evolutionary than revolutionary.
As change slowed, companies gained the confidence to invest for the longer term. They began to combine various parts of the system in new ways to create value for a wider group of users. The massive overbuilding of fiber optic telecom networks and other infrastructure during the frenzy left plenty of cheap capacity, keeping the costs of expansion down. It was a great time to be a businessperson and investor.
In contrast, society did not need a bubble to pop to start excoriating AI. Given that the backlash to tech has been going on for a decade, this seems normal to us. But the AI backlash differs from the general high regard, earlier in the cycle, enjoyed by the likes of Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos, and others who built big tech businesses. The world hates change, and only gave tech a pass in the ‘80s and ‘90s because it all still seemed reversible: it could be made to go away if it turned out badly. This gave the early computer innovators some leeway to experiment. Now that everyone knows computers are here to stay, AI is not allowed the same wait-and-see attitude. It is seen aspartof the ICT revolution.
Perez, the economist, breaks each technological wave into four predictable phases: irruption, frenzy, synergy, and maturity. Each has a characteristic investment profile.
The middle two, frenzy and synergy, are the easy ones for investors. Frenzy is when everyone piles in and investors are rewarded for taking big risks on unproven ideas, culminating in the bubble, when paper profits disappear. When rationality returns, the synergy phase begins, as companies make their products usable and productive for a wide array of users. Synergy pays those who are patient, picky, and can bring more than just money to the table.
Irruption and maturity are more difficult to invest in.
Investing in the 1970s was harder than it might look in hindsight. To invest from 1971 through 1975, you had to be either a true believer or a conglomerator with a knuckle-headed diversification strategy. Intel was a great investment, though it looked at first like a previous-wave electronics company. MOS Technologies was founded in 1969 to compete with Texas Instruments but sold a majority of itself to Allen-Bradley to stay afloat. Zilog was funded in 1975 by Exxon (Exxon!). Apple was a great investment, but it had none of the hallmarks of what VCs look for, as the PC was still a solution in search of a problem.
It was later irruption, in the early 1980s, when great opportunities proliferated: PC makers (Compaq, Dell), software and operating systems (Microsoft, Electronic Arts, Adobe), peripherals (Seagate), workstations (Sun), and computer stores (Businessland), among others. If you invested in the winners, you did well. But there was still more money than ideas, which meant that it was no golden age for investing. By 1983, there were more than 70 companies competing in the disk drive sector alone, and valuations collapsed. There were plenty of people whose fortunes were established in the 1970s and 1980s, and many VCs made their names in that era. But the biggest advantage to being an irruption-stage investor was building institutional knowledge to invest early and well in the frenzy and synergy phases.
Investing in the maturity phase is even more difficult. In irruption, it’s hard to see what will happen; in maturity, nothing much happens at all. The uncertainty about what will work and how customers and society will react is almost gone. Things are predictable, and everyone acts predictably.
The lack of dynamism allows the successful synergy companies to remain entrenched (see: the Nifty 50 and FAANG), but growth becomes harder. They start to enter each other’s markets, conglomerate, raise prices, and cut costs. The era of products priced to entice new customers ends, and quality suffers. The big companies continue to embrace the idea of revolutionary innovation, but feel the need to control how their advances are used. R&D spending is redirected from product and process innovation toward increasingly fruitless attempts to find ways to extend the current paradigm. Companies frame this as a drive to win, but it’s really a fear of losing.
Innovation can happen during maturity, sometimes spectacularly. But because these innovations only find support if they fit into the current wave’s paradigm, they are easily captured in the dominant companies’ gravity wells. This means making money as an entrepreneur or investor in them is almost impossible. Generative AI is clearly being captured by the dominant ICT companies, which raises the question of whether this time will be different for inventors and investors—a different question from whether AI itself is a revolutionary technology.
Shipping containerization was a late-waveinnovation that changed the world, kicked off our modern era of globalization, resulted in profound changes to society and the economy, and contributed to rapid growth in well-being. But there were, perhaps, only one or two people who made real money investing in it.
The year 1956 was late in the previous wave. But that year, the company soon to be known as SeaLand revolutionized freight shipping with the launch of the first containership, the Ideal-X. SeaLand’s founder, Malcom McLean, had an epiphany that the job to be done by truckers, railroads, and shipping lines was to move goods from shipper to destination, not to drive trucks, fill boxcars, or lade boats. SeaLand allowed freight to transfer seamlessly from one mode to another, saving time, making shipping more predictable, and cutting costs—both the costs of loading, unloading, and reloading, and the cost of a ship sitting idly in port as it was loaded and unloaded.[8]
The benefits of containerization, if it could be made to happen, were obvious. Everybody could see the efficiencies, and customers don’t care how something gets to where they can buy it, as long as it does. But longshoremen would lose work, politicians would lose the votes of those who lost work, port authorities would lose the support of the politicians, federal regulators would be blamed for adverse consequences, railroads might lose freight to shipping lines, shipping lines might lose freight to new shipping lines, and it would all cost a mint. Most thought McLean would never be able to make it work.
McLean squeezed through the cracks of the opposition he faced. He bought and retrofitted war surplus ships, lowering costs. He went after the coastal shipping trade, a dying business in the age of the new interstates, to avoid competition. He set up shop in Newark, NJ, rather than the shipping hub of Hell’s Kitchen, to get buy-in from the port authority and avoid Manhattan congestion. And he made a deal with the New York longshoremen’s union, which was only possible because he was a small player whom they figured was not a threat.
Source:[10]
But competitors and regulators moved too quickly for McLean to seize the few barriers to entry that might have been available to him: domination of the ports, exclusive agreements with shippers or other forms of transportation, standardization on proprietary technology, etc.[9]When it started to look like it might work, around 1965, the obvious advantages of containerization meant that every large shipping line entered the business, and competition took off. Even though containerized freight was less than 1% of total trade by 1968, the number of containerships was already ramping fast.[10]Capacity outstripped demand for years.
The increase in competition led to a rate war, which led to squeezed profits, which in turn led to consolidation and cartels. Meanwhile, the cost of building ever-larger container ships and the port facilities to deal with them meant the business became hugely capital intensive. McLean saw the writing on the wall and sold SeaLand to R.J. Reynolds in January 1969. He was, perhaps, the only entrepreneur to get out unscathed.
It took a long time for the end-to-end vision to be realized. But around 1980, a dramatic drop began in the cost of sea freight.[11]This contributed to a boom in international trade,[12]and allowed manufacturers to move away from higher-wage to lower-wage countries, making containerization irreversible.
Source:[11]
Some people did make money, of course; someone always does. McLean did, as did shipping magnate Daniel Ludwig, who had invested $8.5 million in SeaLand’s predecessor, McLean Industries, at $8.50 per share in 1965 and sold in 1969 for $50 per share.[13]Shipbuilders made money, too: between 1967 and 1972, some $10 billion ($80 billion in 2025 dollars) was spent building containerships. The contractors that built the new container ports also made money. And, later, shipping lines that consolidated and dominated the business, like Maersk and Evergreen, became very large. But, “for R.J. Reynolds, and for other companies that had chased fast growth by buying into container shipping in the late 1960s, their investments brought little but disappointment.”[14]Aside from McLean and Ludwig, it is hard to find anyone who became rich from containerization itself, because competition and capex costs made it hard to grow fast or achieve high margins.
Source:[12]
The business ended up being dominated primarily by the previous incumbents, and the margins went to the companies shipping goods, not the ones they shipped through. Companies like IKEA benefited from cheap shipping, going from a provincial Scandinavian company in 1972 to the world’s largest furniture retailer by 2008; container shipping was a perfect fit for IKEA’s flat-pack furniture. Others, like Walmart, used the predictability enabled by containerization to lower inventory and its associated costs.
With hindsight, it’s easy to see how you could have invested in containerization: not in the container shipping industry itself, but in the industries that benefited from containerization. But even here, the success of companies like Walmart, Costco, and Target was coupled with the failure of others. The fallout from containerization set Sears and Woolworth on downward spirals, put the final nail in the coffin of Montgomery Ward and A&P, and drove Macy’s into bankruptcy before it was rescued and downsized by Federated. Meanwhile, in North Carolina, “the furniture capital of the world,” furniture makers tried to compete with IKEA by importing cheap pieces from China. They ended up being replaced by their suppliers.[15]
If there had been more time to build moats, there might have been a few dominant containerization companies, and the people behind them would be at the top of the Forbes 400, while their investors would be legendary. But moats take time to build and, unlike the personal computer, the adoption of containerization wasn’t a surprise—every business with interests at stake had a strategic plan immediately.
The economist Joseph Schumpeter said “perfect competition is and always has been temporarily suspended whenever anything new is being introduced.”[16]But containerization shows this isn’t true at theendof tech waves. And because there is no economic profit during perfect competition, there is no money to be made by innovators during maturity. Like containerization, the introduction of AI did not lead to a period of protected profits for its innovators. It led to an immediate competitive free-for-all.
Let’s grant that generative AI is revolutionary(but also that, as is becoming increasingly clear, this particular tech is now already in an evolutionary stage). It will create a lot of value for the economy, and investors hope to capture some of it. When, who, and how depends on whether AI is the end of the ICT wave, or the beginning of a new one.
If AI had started a new wave, there would have been an extended period of uncertainty and experimentation. There would have been a population of early adopters experimenting with their own models. When thousands or millions of tinkerers use the tech to solve problems in entirely new ways, its uses proliferate. But because they are using models owned by the big AI companies, their ability to fully experiment is limited to what’s allowed by the incumbents, who have no desire to permit an extended challenge to the status quo.
This doesn’t mean AIcan’tstart the next technological revolution. It might, if experimentation becomes cheap, distributed and permissionless—like Wozniak cobbling together computers in his garage, Ford building his first internal combustion engine in his kitchen, or Trevithick building his high-pressure steam engine as soon as James Watt’s patents expired. When any would-be innovator can build and train an LLM on their laptop and put it to use in any way their imagination dictates, it might be the seed of the next big set of changes—something revolutionary rather than evolutionary. But until and unless that happens, there can be no irruption.
AI is instead the epitome of the ICT wave. The computing visionaries of the 1960s set out to build a machine that could think, which their successors eventually did, by extending gains in algorithms, chips, data, and data center infrastructure. Like containerization, AI is an extension of something that came before, and therefore no one is surprised by what it can and will do. In the 1970s, it took time for people to wrap their heads around the desirability of powerful and ubiquitous computing. But in 2025, machines that think better than previous machines are easy for people to understand.
Consider the extent to which the progress of AI rhymes with the business evolution of containerization:
In the “AI rhymes” column, the first four items are already underway. How you should invest depends on whether you believe Nos. 5–7 are next.
Economists are predicting thatAI will increase global GDP somewhere between 1%[17]to more than 7%[18]over the next decade, which is $1–7 trillion of new value created. The big question is where that money will stick as it flows through the value chain.
Most AI market overviews have a score or more categories, breaking each of them into customer and industry served. But these will change dramatically over the next few years. You could, instead, just follow the money to simplify the taxonomy of companies:
What the history of containerization suggests is that, if you aren’t already an investor in a model company, you shouldn’t bother. Sam Altman and a few other early movers may make a fortune, as McLean and Ludwig did. But the huge costs of building and running a model, coupled with intense competition, means there will, in the end, be only a few companies, each funded and owned by the largest tech companies. If you’re already an investor, congratulations: There will be consolidation, so you might get an exit.
Domain-specific models—like Cursor or Harvey—will be part of the consolidation. These are probably the most valuable models. But fine-tuning is relatively cheap, and there are big economies of scope. On the other hand, just as Google had to buy Invite Media in 2010 to figure out how to sell to ad agencies, domain-specific model companies that have earned the trust of their customers will be prime acquisition targets. And although it seems possible that models which generate things other than language—like Midjourney or Runway—might use their somewhat different architecture to carve out a separate technological path, the LLM companies have easily entered this space as well. Whether this applies to companies like Osmo remains to be seen.
While it’s too late to invest in the model companies, the profusion of those using the models to solve specific problems is ongoing: Perplexity, InflectionAI, Writer, Abridge, and a hundred others. But if any of these become very valuable, the model companies will take their earnings, either through discriminatory pricing or vertical integration. Success, in other words, will mean defeat—always a bad thesis. At some point, model companies and app companies will converge: There will simply be AI companies, and only a few of them. There will be some winners, as always, but investments in the app layer as a whole will lose money.
The same caveat applies, however: If an app company can build a customer base or an amazing team, it might be acquired. But these companies aren’t really technology companies at all; they are building a market on spec and have to be priced as such. A further caveat is that there will be investors who make a killing arbitraging FOMO-panicked acquirors willing to massively overpay. But this is not really “investing.”
There might be an investment opportunity in companies that manage the interface between the AI giants and their customers, or protect company data from the model companies—like Hugging Face or Glean—because these businesses are by nature independent of the models. But no analogue in the post-containerization shipping market became very large. Even the successful intermediation companies in the AI space will likely end up mid-sized because the model companies will not allow them to gain strategic leverage—another consequence of the absence of surprise.
When an industry is going to be bigbut there is uncertainty about how it will play out, it often makes sense to swim upstream to the industry’s suppliers. In the case of AI, this means the chip providers, data companies, and cloud/data center companies: SambaNova, Scale AI, and Lambda, as well as those that have been around for a long time, like Nvidia and Bloomberg.
The case for data is mixed. General data—i.e., things most people know, including everything anyone knew more than, say, 10 years ago, and most of what was learned after that—is a commodity. There may be room for a few companies to do the grunt work of collating and tagging it, but since the collating and tagging might best be done by AI itself, there will not be a lot of pricing leverage. Domain-specific models will need specialist data, and other models will try to answer questions about the current moment. Specific, timely, and hard to reproduce data will be valuable. This is not a new market, of course—Bloomberg and others have done well by it. A more concentrated customer base will lower prices for this data, while wider use will raise revenues. On balance, this will probably be a plus for the industry, though not a huge one. There will be new companies built, but only a couple worth investing in.
The high capex of AI companies will primarily be spent with the infrastructure companies. These companies are already valued with this expectation, so there won’t be an upside surprise. But consider that shipbuilding benefited from containerization from 1965 until demand collapsed after about 1973.[19]If AI companies consolidate or otherwise act in concert, even a slight downturn that forces them to conserve cash could turn into a serious, sudden, and long-lasting decline in infrastructure spending. This would leave companies like Nvidia and its emerging competitors—who must all make long-term commitments to suppliers and for capacity expansion—unable to lower costs to match the new, smaller market size. Companies priced for an s-curve are overpriced if there’s a peak and decline.
Source:[19]
All of which means that investors shouldn’t swim upstream, but fish downstream: companies whose products rely on achieving high-quality results from somewhat ambiguous information will see increased productivity and higher profits. These sectors include professional services, healthcare, education, financial services, and creative services, which together account for between a third and a half of global GDP and have not seen much increased productivity from automation. AI can help lower costs, but as with containerization, how individual businesses incorporate lower costs into their strategies—and what they decide to do with the savings—will determine success. To put it bluntly, using cost savings to increase profits rather than grow revenue is a loser’s game.
The companies that will benefit most rapidly are those whose strategies are already conditional on lowering costs. IKEA’s longtime strategy was to sell quality furniture for low prices and make it up on volume. After containerization made it possible for them to go worldwide, IKEA became the world’s largest retailer and Ingvar Kamprad (the IK of IKEA) became a billionaire. Similarly, Walmart, whose strategy was high volume and low prices in underserved markets, benefited from both cost savings and just-in-time supply chains, allowing increased product variety and lower inventory costs.
Today’s knowledge-work companies that already prioritize the same values are the least risky way to bet on AI, but new companies will form or re-form with a high-volume, low-cost strategy, just as Costco did in the early 1980s. New companies will compete with the incumbents, but with a clean slate and hindsight. Regardless, there are few barriers to entry, so each of these firms will face stiff competition and operate in fragmented markets. Experienced management and flawless execution will be key.
Being an entrepreneur will be a fabulous proposition in these sectors. Being an investor will be harder. Companies will not need much private capital—IKEA never needed to raise risk capital, and Costco raised only one round in 1983 before going public in 1985—because implementing cost-savings technology is not capital intensive. As with containerization, there will be a long lag between technology trigger and the best investments. The opportunities will be later.
Stock pickers will also make money, but they need to be choosy. At the high end of projections, an additional 7% in GDP growth over 10 years within one third of the economy gives a tailwind of only about 2% per year to these companies—even less if productivity growth from older ICT products abates. The primary value shift will be to companies that are embracing the strategic implications of AI from companies that are not, the way Walmart benefited from Sears, which took advantage of cheaper goods prices but did not reinvent itself.
Consumers, however, will be the biggest beneficiaries. Previous waves of mechanization benefited labor productivity in manufacturing, driving prices down and saving consumers money. But increased labor productivity in manufacturing also led to higher manufacturing wages. Wages in services businesses had to rise to compete, even though these businesses did not benefit from productivity gains. This caused the price of services to rise.[20]The share of household spending on food and clothing went from 55% in 1918 to 16% in 2023,[21]but the cost of knowledge-intensive services like healthcare and education have grown well above inflation.
Something similar will happen with AI: Knowledge-intensive services will get cheaper, allowing consumers to buy more of them, while services that require person-to-person interaction will get more expensive, taking up a greater percentage of household spending. This points to obvious opportunities in both. But the big news is that most of the new value created by AI will be captured by consumers, who should see a wider variety of knowledge-intensive goods at reasonable prices, and wider and more affordable access to services like medical care, education, and advice.
There is nothing better than the beginning of a new wave, when the opportunities to envision, invent, and build world-changing companies leads to money, fame, and glory. But there is nothing more dangerous for investors and entrepreneurs than wishful thinking. The lessons learned from investing in tech over the last 50 years are not the right ones to apply now. The way to invest in AI is to think through the implications of knowledge workers becoming more efficient, to imagine what markets this efficiency unlocks, and to invest in those. For decades, the way to make money was to bet on what the new thing was. Now, you have to bet on the opportunities it opens up.

Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday forlandmark talks in China.
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.
At least four people were killed in a Russian drone attack on the southern city of Odesa on Wednesday, according to Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

In Kiew ist die Stimmung vor den beiden Treffen heute - in Berlin und in China - eher zurückhaltend. Risiken sehen sie insbesondere bei dem Dreigipfel in Shenzhen. Sie fordern Einheit und Entschlossenheit.
Konkrete gemeinsame Schritte im Verhandlungsprozess mit Russland wolle man ausarbeiten. So formulierte Anfang der Woche der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj seine Erwartungen an das Treffen der Koalition der Willigen in Berlin.
Waffen, Geld, Hilfe - so beschreibt Oleksandr in Kiew seine Erwartungen. Und Studentin Anna meint: "Als Ukrainerin wünsche ich mir Sicherheit und Sicherheitsgarantien." Oleksandr fügt hinzu: "Seid entschlossener, ernster. Es scheint, als würdet ihr die Ukraine aufgeben."
Sicherheitsgarantien sind eine zentrale Forderung der Menschen in der Ukraine. Umso wichtiger sei es,dass Europa mit einer Stimme spreche, sagt der ukrainische Diplomat Serhij Korsunskyj. Auch im Hinblick auf das Treffen in China zwischen US-Präsident Donald Trump, Russlands Machthaber Wladimir Putin und dem chinesischen Staatschef Xi Jinping.
18.11.2026
Die Ukraine braucht dringend Geld - den Großteil soll die EU nach Willen der Kommission übernehmen.mehr
Korsunskyj fordert Einheit: "Wir sehen, dass einzelne europäische Länder bei einzelnen Besuchen versuchen, sich mit den Chinesen zu einigen. Aber das ist nicht richtig. Europa sollte mit einer Stimme sprechen."
Politische Beobachter in der Ukraine haben jedoch geringe Erwartungen an das Treffen in China. Es sei vor allem eine Möglichkeit für Russlands Machthaber Putin, sich international zu inszenieren, meint Politikexperte Oleksandr Krajew.
Für Putin sei das Ganze ein Versuch, in die internationale Diplomatie zurückzukehren, aus der er immer wieder ausgeschlossen war. "Der Gipfel bietet ihm eine Art Wohlfühlatmosphäre. Allerdings sehen wir, dass Xi ihn auf Abstand hält."
19.11.2026
Die Positionen von Xi, Trump und Putin zu Themen nuklearer Abrüstung, Iran oder Ukraine klaffen auseinander.mehr
Und dennoch liege für die Ukraine eine Gefahr in dem Treffen der drei Staatschefs, meint Diplomat Korsunskyi. Denn russlandfreundliche Kräfte in Europa würden den Gipfel in China kommunikativ nutzen, um in Zukunft eine engere Kooperation Europas mit Russland zu fordern. "Die AfD in Deutschland wird nicht eine Minute zögern, dieses Thema anzusprechen. Das Treffen wird von den oppositionellen Kräften in Europa ausgenutzt werden."
Es sollen keine Entscheidungen über die Ukraine ohne die Ukraine getroffen werden. Das betont der ukrainische Außenminister Andrij Sybiha in Kiew. Die USA und China hätten großen Einfluss auf Russland und sollten diesen nutzen, um ein Ende des Krieges gegen die Ukraine näherzubringen, fordert Sybiha. "Druck, Druck auf Putin. Die USA und China verfügen über die Möglichkeiten, diesen Druck auszuüben, damit der Krieg beendet wird."

Stop guessing why CI failed. Reproduce it locally.
Stop guessing why CI failed. Reproduce it locally.
Paste a failed GitHub Actions run URL. FailTrace finds the job and step that failed, matches them to the
workflow file at that exact commit, pulls the failure out of the logs, and tells you what stands between
you and reproducing it on your machine.
Status: early development.All three commands work.reprocovers Linux jobs whose failing step is
arun:script. See theroadmapandlimitations.
actruns your workflows locally, and it's great at that. FailTrace
answers a different question:why did this particular run fail, and can I make it fail the same way here?
Real output for a failedprometheus/prometheusrun (trimmed):
The log ends with hundreds of lines ofgo.sumdiff. FailTrace centres the excerpt on the first error
line so you see the cause,go mod tidychanginggo.mod, instead of the noise after it.
macOS and Linux, using the install script. It downloads the latest release for your platform and
verifies its SHA-256 checksum:
It installs to/usr/local/binif that's writable, otherwise to~/.local/bin. SetFAILTRACE_INSTALL_DIRto choose, orFAILTRACE_VERSION=v0.1.0to pin a release.
Prebuilt binariesfor macOS, Linux and Windows (amd64 and arm64) are on thereleases page, with achecksums.txt.

From source:
Colour output turns off automatically when stdout is not a terminal, or whenNO_COLORis set.
FailTrace needs a GitHub token, even for public repositories, because the logs API requires one. It looks in
this order:
Private repositories need a token that can read Actions on that repo. GitHub Enterprise Server URLs work too:
the API base becomeshttps://<host>/api/v3.
Run context:workflow, event, branch, commit, attempt.
Job → workflow mapping:finds the job definition, including jobs named liketest (ubuntu-latest, 1.22)orLint ${{ matrix.tool }}, and recovers the matrix values.
Runner:the requested label and the actual runner image and version, from the log.
Failed step:its definition (run,uses,with,env, shell, working directory). The command
shown is the one printed in the log, with expressions already filled in.
Diagnosis:exit code, error annotations, failing test names (Go, pytest, Jest, Vitest, Cargo, RSpec),
and a category:
Reproduction notes:anything that makes a local repro harder. That means service containers, job
containers, secrets the step uses, reusable workflows, and macOS or Windows runners.
It also explains edge cases instead of failing silently: runs that failed before any job started, dynamic
workflows with no file in the repo, and logs that have expired.
failtrace planworks out how to reproduce the failed job locally and prints the plan. It doesn't run
anything yet.
Real output for a failedpytest-dev/pytestjob (trimmed):
How the plan is built:
Theverdictisready(nothing known to be missing),partial(it can run, but some parts are
approximated or missing) orblocked(the failing step is an action, not a script, so it can't be replayed
yet).
Supported setup actions:actions/setup-go,setup-node,setup-python,setup-java,setup-dotnet,ruby/setup-ruby,dtolnay/rust-toolchain,actions-rust-lang/setup-rust-toolchain,pnpm/action-setup,pnpm/setup,astral-sh/setup-uv,oven-sh/setup-bunanddenoland/setup-deno.
failtrace reprobuilds the plan and runs it in Docker, then compares the result with CI's failure.
You need Docker (Docker Desktop, colima, OrbStack, …) and git.
Real output for a failedstretchr/testifyrun, wherego vetfailed
under Gooldstable. FailTrace resolvedoldstableto the exact Go 1.26.9 build CI used, checked out the
PR merge commit CI tested, and replayed the steps:
Without--platform, the job runs aslinux/amd64like CI did. On an Apple silicon Mac that means
emulation: the same reproduction took about 9 minutes instead of 40 seconds, with the same verdict.
What happens:
Environment image.The plan's base image, plus the packages every GitHub Ubuntu runner has
(git, curl, build tools, python3, jq, sudo, …), plus the toolchains. Go, Node and Python are the same
buildssetup-go,setup-nodeandsetup-pythondownload, installed under/opt/hostedtoolcachewhere CI keeps them. uv, pnpm and Rust are installed from their releases. The image is tagged by a hash
of its contents, so it's only built once per environment.
Workspace.The exact commit CI tested is fetched on your machine the wayactions/checkoutdoes
it, with the same fetch depth, and mounted at the same path as on the runner
(/home/runner/work/<repo>/<repo>, or/__w/...for container jobs). If GitHub has since replaced a
pull request's merge commit, the merge is recreated locally.
Services.Service containers start in the job container's network namespace, solocalhost:5432andpostgres:5432both work, and FailTrace waits for their health checks.
Steps.Run steps replay in order with the shell, environment and working directory CI used.$GITHUB_ENVand$GITHUB_PATHcarry over between steps. The failing step's output streams live.
Verdict.
A list of known differences from CI comes with every verdict.
The setup steps run once, then the failing step runs N times in the same container, so repeats are
cheap. If it fails only some of the time, the verdict isflaky("the step failed in 3 of 10 runs").
Go's test cache is bypassed for these runs (GOFLAGS=-count=1). Otherwisego testwould replay a cached
pass and hide the flakiness.
When the run finishes,--shellopens a shell where the failing step ran: same directory, environment,
toolchains and services. It prints the command that re-runs the step:
If an earlier step diverged, the shell opens at that step instead. The container is removed when you exit,
unless you pass--keep.
--report repro.mdwrites a Markdown report to paste into an issue or pull request. It includes the
verdict, a CI-vs-local table, environment, differences, every step's result, and the output of the failing
step from both sides.--report -prints it instead of the terminal summary. Seedocs/example-report.md, generated from the stretchr/testify run above with--runs 3.
--source .swaps the commit CI tested for your local working tree, so you can check a fix on the same
CI step before pushing it. FailTrace copies the tree'sHEADplus your uncommitted and untracked files
into the workspace as one extra commit, so the checkout is clean the way it is in CI. Files your.gitignoreexcludes, such as.envornode_modules, are left out. Your working tree is only read.
Setup steps, toolchains and services stay as CI had them.
From the testify run above, after fixing the twogo veterrors without committing:
repro's exit status matches the failing step, so scripts and coding agents can loop on it without
parsing the output:
For details,--jsonprints the plan and the result: verdict, reasons, the CI and local failures, and
every step's outcome.
Safety.reproruns the repository's code, including code from a pull request, inside a container on
your machine. The container sees only the workspace, has no access to your home directory or the Docker
socket, and gets no secrets unless you pass them with--secret NAME. The value is read from your
environment, so it never appears in your shell history or the process list. Only reproduce runs whose
code you're comfortable executing.
Limitations.These are reported instead of silently ignored:
CI runs all of the above on every pull request. To publish a release, push a version tag (git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0);release.ymlbuilds and uploads the binaries.

articles_used.title: Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
articles_used.summary_raw: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.
articles_used.full_text:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO wasthe election's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk wasspeaking virtually,externalat the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.
In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governorpromised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.

One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According toBBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.

articles_used.title: Ukraine-Gipfel in Berlin: Mit Diplomatie und Druck
articles_used.summary_raw: Heute kommen knapp 30 Staats- und Regierungschefs nach Berlin, sie gehören zu den wichtigsten Unterstützern der Ukraine. Vom Treffen soll ein klares Signal ausgehen: Die Ukraine kann weiter auf Hilfe zählen. Von Christina Nagel.
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 19.11.2026 • 05:05 Uhr
Heute kommen knapp 30 Staats- und Regierungschefs nach Berlin, sie gehören zu den wichtigsten Unterstützern der Ukraine. Vom Treffen soll ein klares Signal ausgehen: Die Ukraine kann weiter auf Hilfe zählen.
Im Kanzleramt ist man Betrieb gewohnt. So viele Staats- und Regierungschefs auf einmal hat es hier allerdings bisher noch nicht gegeben. Insgesamt werden 40 Delegationen am Gipfeltreffen der wichtigsten Ukraine-Unterstützer teilnehmen. Darunter die Spitzen der NATO und der Europäischen Union. Auch der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj wird erwartet.
Allein schon von der Größe des Treffens soll ein Signal ausgehen: Die Unterstützer der Ukraine halten Kurs, auch im fünften Kriegswinter. Man werde, so formuliert es Kanzler Friedrich Merz, die Ukraine weiter mit aller Kraft unterstützen und den Druck auf Moskau erhöhen - bis Russland zu ernsthaften Verhandlungen bereit sei.
Interview11.11.2026
Russland strebt nach Hegemonie in Europa, sagt eine Sicherheitsexpertin. Nun übernähmen die USA ihre Logik.mehr
Dass die Europäer bei solchen Verhandlungen eine Rolle spielen müssen, steht für den Kanzler außer Frage: "Zentrale Elemente einer Friedenslösung, sei es zu Sanktionen oder zur Sicherheitsarchitektur, können nur mit uns Europäern gelöst werden; das wissen alle Beteiligten sehr genau."
Trotzdem ist die Sorge groß, dass es einen solchen Deal über die Köpfe der Ukrainer und Europäer hinweg geben könnte. Entsprechend genau wird das Treffen von US-Präsident Donald Trump mit dem russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin und Chinas Staatschef Xi Jinping am Rande des Gipfels der Asiatisch-Pazifischen Wirtschaftsgemeinschaft (APEC) im chinesischen Shenzhen beobachtet. Denn auch sie wollen über die Ukraine reden.
18.11.2026
Auf dem APEC-Gipfel in Shenzhen kommt es erstmals zu einem Dreier-Treffen von Xi, Trump und Putin.mehr
Um aus der Abhängigkeit herauszukommen, drängt nicht nur der finnische Präsident Alexander Stubb darauf, dass sich die Europäer selbst stärker diplomatisch einbringen. Er hatte unlängst gemeinsam mit dem norwegischen Regierungschef Jonas Gahr Storemit Putin telefoniert.
Bei seinem Besuch am Dienstag in Berlin stellteStubbklar: "Wenn man nicht über Frieden spricht, wird man auch keinen Frieden bekommen." Es brauche Dialog, Austausch und Diplomatie - und eine klare Agenda für mögliche Gespräche mit Russland.
Beim Treffen im Kanzleramt sollen Positionen und Verhandlungsschritte abgestimmt werden. Auch mit den beiden US-SondergesandtenSteve Witkoffund Jared Kushner. Dabei geht es um zentrale Fragen: um eine Waffenruhe, um Territorium und Sicherheitsgarantien sowie um eine neue europäische Sicherheitsordnung für eine Zeit nach dem Krieg.
11.11.2026
In Abu Dhabi gehen die von den USA vermittelten Gespräche über ein Ende des Kriegs gegen die Ukraine weiter.mehr
Ob und wann es zu Verhandlungen kommt, bei denen die Europäer mit am Tisch sitzen, bleibt allerdings offen. Kreml-Berater Juri Uschakow hatte erklärt, dass eine Erweiterung des bestehenden Formats nicht mit der russischen Seite abgestimmt worden sei.
Aussagen wie diese bestärken Befürchtungen von Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier, dass Russland weiterhin nicht zu ernsthaften Verhandlungen über ein Ende des Krieges bereit sei. Umso wichtiger sei es, Sanktionen aufrechtzuerhalten, um weiter Druck auf Russland auszuüben, betonte er am Dienstag im Beisein des finnischen Präsidenten. Und: die Ukraine weiter zu unterstützen. Militärische Stärke sei nötig, um diplomatischen Bemühungen die nötige Kraft zu verleihen.
17.11.2026
Der Ukraine droht angesichts massiver russischer Angriffe ein harter Winter. Deutschland zahlt für US-Patriotssysteme.mehr
Deutschland und Norwegen haben in dieser Woche bereits ein weiteres Unterstützungspaket angekündigt. Von dem zur Verfügung gestellten Geld sollen nach Angaben von Verteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius weitere Flugabwehrsysteme für die Ukraine in den USA gekauft werden.
Nicht nur der Verteidigungsminister drängt darauf, dass sich mehr Verbündete an den Ukraine-Hilfen beteiligen, trotz knapper Kassen. Die Unterstützung der Ukraine sei keine Charity-Veranstaltung, sagte Pistorius in Brüssel. "Es geht hier um weit mehr als um Solidarität. Es geht um die Sicherheit von Europa und es geht darum, den russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin aufzuhalten und in die Schranken zu weisen."
18.11.2026
Die Ukraine braucht dringend Geld - den Großteil soll die EU nach Willen der Kommission übernehmen.mehr
Damit das gelingt, das wird der ukrainische Präsident heute in Berlin einmal klar machen, braucht die Ukraine weiter Unterstützung. Auch finanziell. Wolodymyr Selenskyj hat bereits angekündigt, dass die Ukraine allein für das kommende Jahr zusätzliche 70 Milliarden Euro benötigt.
Auch über weitere Hilfen, damit die Menschen trotz der massiven Attacken auf ukrainische Energieanlagenüber den Winter kommen, wird heute in Berlin geredet werden. In der Hoffnung, dass möglichst viele der anreisenden Gipfelteilnehmer der Ukraine nicht nur verbal den Rücken stärken, sondern auch materiell.

articles_used.title: AI giant Anthropic valued at up to $1.5tn ahead of stock market debut
articles_used.summary_raw: The firm started just five years ago and is now one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence.
articles_used.full_text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has quickly become a big name in the tech industry
Anthropic has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5tn (£1.14tn) as its shares are set to start trading on the stock market on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
Anthropic's stock market debut will make it the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public. It will also mark a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which facesquestions over whether the huge amounts of moneybeing poured into the technology will be profitable.
The firm said earlier this month it would offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.
But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.
Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world'smost highly valued stock debutwhen it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX sharesfell significantly in price.
As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceXraised in June.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.
Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.
The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollarsin financial obligationscome due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.
While nearly every other major tech company is pouringhuge amounts of moneyinto the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Anthropic was started by agroup of co-founders, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.
Itrefused to complywith a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.
CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present athreat to human existence.
The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.
Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.
Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Claude is Anthropic's widely-used AI chatbot
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."
But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent oncontroversial data centresand funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.
The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

articles_used.title: Anthropic-Ausgabepreis bei Börsengang bei 83 Dollar je Aktie
articles_used.summary_raw: Zum ersten Mal geht mit Anthropic ein maßgebliches KI-Unternehmen an den Markt. Der Börsengang könnte der größte der Welt werden - und sogar den bisherigen Rekord von Elon Musk mit SpaceX hinter sich lassen. Von G. Ucar.
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 19.11.2026 • 04:14 Uhr
Zum ersten Mal geht mit Anthropic ein maßgebliches KI-Unternehmen an den Markt. Der Börsengang könnte der größte der Welt werden - und sogar den bisherigen Rekord von Elon Musk mit SpaceX hinter sich lassen.
Es wirkt fast bizarr:Dario Amodei, der CEO von Anthropic, sitzt bei einer Werbeveranstaltung vor Investoren und warnt. Ausgerechnet vor der Technologie, die sein Unternehmen herstellt. Er warnt vor Künstlicher Intelligenz: "Diese KI-Agenten werden unglaublich schnell immer leistungsfähiger. Was uns bei der Entwicklung der Technologie tatsächlich einschränkt, uns bei der internen Bereitstellung behindert und auch unsere Kunden einschränkt, ist, das auf sichere Weise zu tun. Wir wollen nicht, dass diese Agenten durchdrehen."
Der Börsengang von Anthropic steht kurz bevor. Er könnte gewaltig werden. Tech-Star Elon Musk sammelte erst im Juni bei einem Mega-Börsengang 75 Milliarden Dollar ein. KI-Gigant Anthropic wird diese Summe übertreffen - mit einen Aktienwert von 83 Dollar pro Aktie. Mit 26 Milliarden eingenommenen Dollar durch Großinvestoren und den 980 Millionen Aktien - davon stammen rund 956 Millionen direkt vom Unternehmen - könnten so also für Anthropic 107 Milliarden Dollar zusammenkommen -mehr als für SpaceX. Der Börsenwert würde somit bei rund 1,5 Billionen Dollar liegen.
Der Börsenprospekt, der Anleger eigentlich animieren soll, Geld in das Unternehmen zu investieren, schildert fast 100 Seiten lang Risiken undGefahren durch KI. Wie passt das zusammen? Erin Griffith, Tech-Expertin der New York Times, erklärt im Podcast The Daily: "Das Unternehmen sieht das nicht als Widerspruch. Sondern als sich ergänzend. Sie sagen: 'Wir entwickeln die sicherste aller KIs - und wir gehen jetzt an die Börse'. Die Öffentlichkeit kann jetzt also ein Teil davon sein und in die sicherste Variante von KI investieren. Das ist ihr Verkaufsargument."
10.11.2026
Das KI-Unternehmen Anthropic hat Details seiner Börsenpläne veröffentlicht.mehr
Anthropic verspricht seinen Kunden einen besonders verantwortungsvollen Umgang mit KI und will sich dadurch von Konkurrenten wie Google oder OpenAI unterscheiden. Gleichzeitig will das Unternehmen aber auch profitabel für Investoren sein. Bisherige Umsatz-Zahlen sehen vielversprechend aus - an ihnen lässt sich der Boom der letzten Jahre in der KI-Branche ablesen.
Das Wachstum bei Anthropic hat selbst Tech-Expertin Griffith verblüfft. "Ich habe es noch nie so vertikal nach oben gehen sehen. Im dritten Quartal dieses Jahres hatten sie 17 Milliarden US-Dollar Umsatz - und das ist ein Unternehmen, das noch vor fünf Jahren gar keinen Umsatz hatte."
31.07.2026
Zum zweiten Mal innerhalb weniger Tage kommt es zu einem schwerwiegenden KI-Zwischenfall.mehr
Anthropic wurde 2021 gegründet und ist in wenigen Jahren zum führenden KI-Entwickler geworden. Dabei konzentriert sich das Unternehmen vor allem auf Geschäftskunden, die ihr Sprachmodell "Claude" oder den Coding-Assistenten "Claude Code" in vielen Bereichen nutzen können: zum Analysieren von Dokumenten und Daten, bei der Buchhaltung, fürs Marketing oder sogar bei der Software-Entwicklung.
Griffith sagt: "Die Größe dieses Markts ist nach Ansicht von Anthropic enorm. Sie behaupten, dass sie das Potenzial haben, einen 40-Billionen-Dollar-Markt zu erschließen. Das entspricht dem wirtschaftlichen Wert aller Mitarbeiter, die für ihren Job an einem Schreibtisch sitzen und einen Computer nutzen. Jeder von ihnen könnte potenzieller Kunde ihrer Produkte sein."
Doch um dieses Ziel zu erreichen, muss Anthropic vorerst Unsummen an Geld in den Ausbau von KI-Infrastruktur stecken. Die jährlichen Ausgaben sind ein Vielfaches höher als die Einnahmen. Und das wird auf absehbare Zeit auch so bleiben.
17.09.2026
Forscher in Deutschland relativieren die Warnungen vor KI und nehmen auch die Entwickler in die Pflicht.mehr
Anthropic hat sich verpflichtet, bis 2045 fast 900 Milliarden Dollar in Rechenleistung oder Computer-Chips zu investieren. Genau das könnte ein Risiko für Investoren sein, sagt Griffith: "Wir haben darüber geredet, wie schnell der Umsatz gewachsen ist. Aber er müsste jetzt auch weiterhin so schnell oder sogar noch schneller wachsen, damit Anthropic seinen Verpflichtungen nachkommen kann." Für Investoren sei also die Frage: "Haben sie auf das richtige Pferd im KI-Rennen gesetzt? Oder werden sie am Ende für die vielen Deals aufkommen müssen, die Anthropic nicht zahlen können wird?"
Die Zweifel rund um gehypte KI-Unternehmen werden in letzter Zeit immer größer. Börsendaten zeigen, dass die Investitionsfreude bei Anlegern leicht zurückgeht. Der Widerstand gegen den Bau benötigter Rechenzentren, die Angst vor strenger Regulierung durch die Demokraten im Kongress und auch der Skandal rund um Chiphersteller Nvidia verunsichern. Deshalb gilt der Börsengang von Anthropic auch als Stimmungstest für die gesamte KI-Branche.

segments.headline: Historischer Dreier-Gipfel: Xi, Trump und Putin treffen sich in Shenzhen
segments.narration: Ein außergewöhnliches diplomatisches Ereignis findet heute in Shenzhen statt: Der chinesische Präsident Xi Jinping empfängt den russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin und den ehemaligen US-Präsidenten Donald Trump. Dieses Gipfeltreffen, das am Rande des Asien-Pazifik-Gipfels abgehalten wird, ist ein diplomatisches Meisterstück für China, das sich zunehmend als Gestalter der Weltordnung positioniert. Für Xi ist es eine Gelegenheit, Chinas globalen Einfluss zu demonstrieren, auch wenn er dabei heikle Themen wie den Krieg in der Ukraine und nukleare Abrüstung umschiffen muss. Die Ukraine selbst blickt mit gemischten Gefühlen auf das Treffen: Während man dort Einheit und Entschlossenheit der Verbündeten fordert, befürchtet man, dass Entscheidungen über die Köpfe Kiews hinweg getroffen werden könnten. Gleichzeitig findet in Berlin ein weiteres wichtiges Treffen statt, bei dem europäische Staats- und Regierungschefs ihre Unterstützung für die Ukraine bekräftigen und über weitere Hilfen beraten.
segments.summary_short: Chinas Präsident Xi Jinping trifft sich in Shenzhen mit Wladimir Putin und Donald Trump, ein diplomatisches Manöver, das Chinas globalen Einfluss stärken soll, während gleichzeitig in Berlin europäische Staatschefs über weitere Ukraine-Hilfen beraten.

segments.headline: Krim-Brücke nach drittem Angriff gesperrt
segments.narration: Apropos Ukraine-Krieg: Die Krim-Brücke, ein wichtiges Symbol und eine logistische Drehscheibe für Russland, wurde zum dritten Mal innerhalb einer Woche angegriffen und ist derzeit für den Verkehr gesperrt. Der von Moskau eingesetzte Verwaltungschef der Krim, Sergej Aksjonow, bestätigte die vorübergehende Einstellung des Zugverkehrs. Die Ukraine hat bereits in den letzten Tagen massive Angriffe auf das Prestigeprojekt von Wladimir Putin durchgeführt, wobei Teile der Brücke schwer beschädigt wurden. Diese Angriffe verdeutlichen die anhaltenden Bemühungen Kiews, russische Versorgungswege zu stören und Druck auf Moskau auszuüben.
segments.summary_short: Die Krim-Brücke wurde zum dritten Mal innerhalb einer Woche angegriffen und ist für den Verkehr gesperrt, was als Rückschlag für Russland im Ukraine-Krieg gilt.

segments.headline: Elon Musk bereut hohe Wahlkampfausgaben nach Republikaner-Niederlage
segments.narration: Wechseln wir das Thema zur US-Politik. Elon Musk äußerte sich kürzlich 'ziemlich dumm' über die Rekordsummen, die er in die US-Zwischenwahlen investiert hatte. Er war der größte Einzelspender für die Republikanische Partei, insbesondere in Texas, wo viele seiner Unternehmen ansässig sind. Trotz seiner erheblichen finanziellen Unterstützung erlitten die Republikaner schwere Niederlagen, und die Demokraten übernahmen die Kontrolle über beide Kammern des US-Kongresses. Musk betonte, nicht Teil der 'Maga'-Bewegung zu sein und zeigte sich enttäuscht über die Ergebnisse seiner Investitionen, die nun auch Auswirkungen auf seine Unternehmen haben könnten, da die Demokraten eine strengere Kontrolle von Technologiekonzernen angekündigt haben.
segments.summary_short: Elon Musk äußerte Bedauern über seine hohen Wahlkampfausgaben für die Republikaner bei den US-Zwischenwahlen, nachdem die Partei deutliche Niederlagen erlitten hatte.

segments.headline: KI-Gigant Anthropic mit Rekordbewertung vor Börsengang
segments.narration: Bleiben wir bei der Wirtschaft, genauer gesagt im Tech-Sektor. Das KI-Unternehmen Anthropic, bekannt für seinen Chatbot Claude, steht kurz vor seinem Börsengang an der Nasdaq und wird voraussichtlich mit bis zu 1,5 Billionen Dollar bewertet. Der Ausgabepreis der Aktien liegt bei 83 Dollar pro Stück. Damit könnte Anthropic der größte Börsengang eines reinen KI-Unternehmens werden und sogar Elon Musks SpaceX in den Schatten stellen. Trotz des großen Interesses gibt es Bedenken hinsichtlich der Rentabilität der KI-Branche und der enormen finanziellen Verpflichtungen, die Anthropic eingehen muss. segments.headline: FailTrace: GitHub Actions-Fehler lokal reproduzieren

Es soll die Fehlersuche in GitHub Actions erheblich vereinfachen. Mit 'FailTrace' kann man einen fehlgeschlagenen GitHub Actions-Lauf lokal reproduzieren, indem man einfach die URL des Runs eingibt. Das Tool analysiert den Fehler, matcht ihn mit der Workflow-Datei und ermöglicht es, die genaue Umgebung nachzubilden.
